body:
Why representation remained disputed

During the 1920s and 1930s, Indian political organisations continued debating how Hindus, Muslims and other communities should share political power in a future independent or self-governing India.

The central problem was that numerical majority, political organisation and community representation were not identical. A party claiming to represent a religious community might not command the support of every member of that community.

Minority safeguards were therefore debated in relation to legislative seats, voting arrangements, provincial autonomy and the powers of the central government.

Attempts at Congress-League compromise

During 1927, Muhammad Ali Jinnah indicated a willingness to abandon separate electorates under certain conditions. These included safeguards for Muslim representation in the Central Legislature and representation proportionate to population in Muslim-majority provinces such as Bengal and Punjab.

Negotiations continued, but the attempt to reach a general constitutional agreement failed in 1928. Opposition to compromises over communal representation, including objections from Hindu Mahasabha figures such as M.R. Jayakar, contributed to the breakdown.

The failure showed that political leaders disagreed not simply over independence from Britain but over the future structure of representative government.

Growing religious political mobilisation

Communal tensions increased in several regions during the 1920s. Religious processions, rival political campaigns and local disputes sometimes resulted in communal riots.

Organisations seeking political support on religious lines often treated the protection of their community as an important objective. Such mobilisation could strengthen demands for safeguards while also making compromise more difficult.

Nevertheless, religious communities were not politically uniform. Muslims supported different parties, including Congress, the Muslim League and regional organisations. Hindu political opinion was similarly divided between Congress, the Hindu Mahasabha and other political groups.

Religion did not determine every political choice

Political support depended on several factors, including class interests, local leadership, regional politics and views about constitutional reform. It is therefore incorrect to assume that every Muslim supported the Muslim League or that every Hindu supported the Hindu Mahasabha.

Muhammad Iqbal and Muslim political autonomy

In 1930, Muhammad Iqbal addressed the Muslim League at Allahabad and argued for political arrangements that would allow Muslim communities to develop according to their cultural and political interests.

He emphasised the importance of Muslim-majority regions and constitutional safeguards. His ideas influenced later discussions of Muslim political autonomy.

However, Iqbal's Allahabad address should not be treated as identical to the final Partition settlement of 1947. Political proposals for regional autonomy and demands for a fully sovereign separate country were not always the same.

The Government of India Act, 1935

The Government of India Act, 1935 provided for provincial autonomy and expanded the system of representative government, although British authority remained substantial.

Provincial elections were held in 1937. Congress performed strongly and formed ministries in 7 of the 11 provinces.

The Muslim League did not establish itself as the dominant Muslim political organisation throughout British India in these elections. Regional political parties remained influential in several Muslim-majority areas.

Congress-League disagreement after the 1937 elections

The Muslim League feared that a future representative system dominated by Congress might not adequately protect Muslim political interests.

A particularly important disagreement occurred in the United Provinces, where the Congress did not accept the League's proposed arrangement for forming a joint provincial ministry.

This disagreement increased political distrust. League leaders increasingly portrayed Congress ministries as evidence of the dangers of majority domination.

Congress, meanwhile, continued to describe itself as a national organisation representing Indians across religious communities. It did not accept the League's claim to exclusive political representation of Muslims.

The importance of 1939

When the Second World War began in September 1939, the British involved India in the war without securing the agreement of elected Indian political leaders.

Congress ministries resigned in protest after the British refused to accept Congress demands concerning India's political future.

The resignations removed Congress provincial governments and created a changed political environment. During the following years, the Muslim League expanded its political activity and sought wider support for its constitutional demands.

Prelims focus

  • 1927: Jinnah indicated conditional willingness to abandon separate electorates.
  • 1928: Attempts at a broader constitutional compromise failed.
  • 1930: Muhammad Iqbal addressed the Muslim League at Allahabad.
  • 1935: Government of India Act provided for provincial autonomy.
  • 1937: Congress formed ministries in 7 of 11 provinces.
  • 1939: Congress ministries resigned during the Second World War.

[NCERT, India and the Contemporary World II, Class 10, Nationalism in India, printed pp. 68–69; NCERT, Our Pasts III, Class 8, Chapter 9, printed pp. 122–126; NCERT, Themes in Indian History Part III, Class 12, Understanding Partition, printed pp. 383–388.]

pictures.caption: Unresolved political safeguards contributed to growing constitutional disagreement.

title: Communal Tensions and Competing Political Demands, 1927–1939

body:
From minority safeguards to the demand for separate political units

In its early years, the Muslim League concentrated on constitutional safeguards and adequate Muslim representation within British India.

During the late 1930s, particularly after the provincial elections of 1937, the League increasingly argued that Muslims constituted a distinct political nation whose interests could not be protected merely through ordinary majority-based representative government.

This position developed into the demand commonly associated with the two-nation theory.

Two-nation theory

In the context of the Partition movement, the two-nation theory was the political argument advanced by the Muslim League that Hindus and Muslims constituted distinct nations and that Muslims required separate political arrangements, ultimately leading to the demand for Pakistan.

The theory was a political claim, not evidence that all Hindus or all Muslims shared identical views. Many Muslims opposed Partition, while Congress rejected the argument that religious identity should determine separate national sovereignty.

The name Pakistan and the Lahore Resolution

The name Pakistan had been proposed earlier by Choudhry Rahmat Ali, a student at Cambridge, in a pamphlet published in 1933. His proposal was not then the official constitutional programme of the Muslim League.

The decisive later development was the Muslim League's Lahore Resolution of March 1940.

The resolution called for Muslim-majority areas in the north-western and eastern zones of British India to be grouped into politically independent units. Its formulation referred to Independent States, with constituent units described as autonomous and sovereign.

The resolution did not explicitly use the word Pakistan. It also did not provide the final territorial boundaries or administrative arrangements that emerged in 1947.

The central distinction

1940: The Muslim League called for independent political arrangements in Muslim-majority north-western and eastern regions.

1947: The Partition settlement established India and Pakistan as 2 separate Dominions.

The later settlement should not be read back into the wording of the 1940 resolution as though every detail had already been settled.

Congress opposition to Partition

The Congress leadership continued to favour an independent India containing different religious communities within a common political framework.

Mahatma Gandhi opposed the division of the country on religious grounds and emphasised Hindu-Muslim unity.

Maulana Abul Kalam Azad, a prominent Muslim Congress leader, opposed the two-nation theory and supported a united India.

Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan, also known as Frontier Gandhi or Badshah Khan, led the Khudai Khidmatgar movement in the North-West Frontier Province and opposed Partition.

These examples demonstrate that support for Muslim political identity did not necessarily require support for a sovereign Pakistan.

Regional parties also maintained distinct political positions. For example, the Unionist Party in Punjab represented important agricultural and landholding interests across religious communities.

Cripps Mission, 1942

During the Second World War, the British government sent Sir Stafford Cripps to India in 1942 with proposals for India's constitutional future.

The proposals offered a framework for dominion status after the war and constitution-making by Indians. They also allowed provinces unwilling to accept the proposed constitution to remain outside the new Union, retaining their existing constitutional position or negotiating a separate constitution with the same Dominion status.

The proposals failed to secure agreement. Congress objected to the absence of an immediate satisfactory transfer of effective power, while the League remained dissatisfied with the arrangements concerning Pakistan.

The failure demonstrated that British promises of future constitutional reform could not resolve the differences between the major political organisations.

Gandhi-Jinnah talks, 1944

In 1944, Gandhi and Jinnah held discussions in an attempt to resolve their differences.

Gandhi proposed a plebiscite of all inhabitants in contiguous Muslim-majority areas to decide separation after independence, while Jinnah insisted on recognition of Muslim nationhood and the political demands associated with Pakistan.

The discussions ended without agreement.

The Wavell Plan and Simla Conference, 1945

In 1945, Viceroy Lord Wavell proposed reorganising his Executive Council to increase Indian participation in central government.

The proposal led to the Simla Conference of 1945, where Congress and League leaders discussed the composition of the proposed government.

A central disagreement concerned the right to nominate Muslim members of the Executive Council. Jinnah argued that the Muslim League should have the exclusive right to nominate Muslim representatives.

Congress rejected this claim because it regarded itself as a national organisation that included Muslim members and leaders.

The conference failed to produce agreement. The dispute revealed a fundamental problem: the parties disagreed not only over the distribution of seats but also over which organisation had the authority to represent particular communities.

Prelims focus

  • 1933: Choudhry Rahmat Ali proposed the name Pakistan.
  • March 1940: Muslim League adopted the Lahore Resolution.
  • 1942: Cripps Mission presented constitutional proposals.
  • 1944: Gandhi-Jinnah talks failed to reach agreement.
  • 1945: Simla Conference associated with the Wavell Plan.
  • Trap: The Lahore Resolution did not explicitly use the word Pakistan or define the final borders of 1947.

[NCERT, Our Pasts III, Class 8, Chapter 9, printed pp. 123–126; NCERT, Themes in Indian History Part III, Class 12, Understanding Partition, printed pp. 385–389; Government of India, Ministry of External Affairs, Indian constitutional documents, Cripps Proposals, 1942; Government of India, Publications Division, Towards Independence, section on the Simla Conference, consulted 22 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: The March 1940 Lahore Resolution concerned separated north-western and eastern Muslim-majority zones, without naming Pakistan or fixing its 1947 borders.
pictures.caption: The Lahore Resolution referred to 2 geographically separated Muslim-majority zones.

title: The Lahore Resolution of 1940 and the Demand for Pakistan

body:
Political negotiations after the Second World War

The end of the Second World War in 1945 created conditions for renewed negotiations over India's independence. British leaders increasingly recognised the need to transfer political power, but the Congress and Muslim League remained divided over the constitutional structure of the future country.

The central disagreement concerned whether India should remain united under a common government or be divided into separate sovereign political units.

The elections of 1945–46

Elections to central and provincial legislatures were held during 1945–46.

Congress performed strongly in general constituencies, while the Muslim League achieved substantial success in seats reserved for Muslims, particularly in the provincial elections of 1946.

These results strengthened the competing political claims of both organisations:

  • Congress: Presented itself as the principal national organisation seeking independence for India as a whole.
  • Muslim League: Used its success in Muslim-reserved constituencies to strengthen its claim to represent Muslim political interests and its demand for Pakistan.

The electoral results did not mean that every Hindu supported Congress or every Muslim supported the League. Nevertheless, they made the dispute over political representation more difficult to resolve.

Appointment of the Cabinet Mission

In March 1946, the British government sent a 3-member Cabinet Mission to India.

Its members were:

  • Lord Pethick-Lawrence: Secretary of State for India.
  • Sir Stafford Cripps: British Cabinet minister involved in constitutional negotiations.
  • A.V. Alexander: British Cabinet minister.

The Mission attempted to secure agreement on a constitutional framework that would permit British withdrawal while addressing competing Congress and League demands.

The Cabinet Mission Statement of 16 May 1946

On 16 May 1946, the Mission announced its constitutional proposals.

The central recommendation was that India should remain united under a constitutional arrangement that gave the provinces substantial autonomy.

The Mission rejected the proposal for transferring power immediately to 2 completely separate sovereign states. Instead, it recommended a Union containing British India and the Indian States, with a limited central government.

Powers of the proposed Union

The proposed Union government would deal with:

  • Foreign affairs.
  • Defence.
  • Communications.

The Union would also have the financial powers required to administer these subjects.

All other subjects and residuary powers were to belong to the provinces. Residuary powers are powers concerning matters not assigned to the Union under the proposed constitutional arrangement.

This would have created a limited central government, rather than a strongly centralised system.

Grouping of provinces

The Cabinet Mission also proposed arrangements under which provinces could form groups and administer certain subjects jointly.

The constitution-making procedure divided provincial representatives into 3 sections:

  • Section A: Madras, Bombay, United Provinces, Bihar, Central Provinces and Orissa.
  • Section B: Punjab, North-West Frontier Province and Sind.
  • Section C: Bengal and Assam.

Under the proposed procedure, representatives of these sections would consider provincial and group constitutions. A province could leave its group by a decision of its legislature after the first general election under the new constitution.

The grouping arrangements were important because the League sought constitutional safeguards for Muslim-majority regions, while Congress opposed arrangements that it believed could undermine national unity or unduly restrict provincial choice.

Constituent Assembly and Interim Government

The Mission also proposed machinery for establishing a Constituent Assembly to frame India's future Constitution.

Provincial representatives were to be chosen through the existing provincial legislatures, while representation of the princely states was to be arranged through negotiations.

The Mission's wider proposals also provided for forming an Interim Government to administer India during the transition from British rule.

The Constituent Assembly and Interim Government were different institutions. The Assembly was intended to prepare the constitutional framework; the Interim Government was intended to perform governmental functions during the transition.

Why the Cabinet Mission Plan failed

Congress and the Muslim League disagreed over the interpretation of the grouping provisions and the freedom of the Constituent Assembly to determine the final constitutional arrangements.

Congress wanted an effective national government and did not accept compulsory political arrangements that could permanently divide the country into religious blocs.

The League wanted strong safeguards for Muslim-majority groups and regarded the grouping system as essential to protecting Muslim political interests.

Although the parties initially engaged with the proposals, their disagreement over implementation became increasingly serious. The League subsequently withdrew its acceptance, and the proposed united constitutional settlement failed.

The essential distinction

The Cabinet Mission Plan of 1946 proposed a united India with a limited Union government and extensive provincial autonomy. It did not recommend the immediate establishment of 2 independent Dominions. That outcome was adopted under the later 3 June Plan and the Indian Independence Act, 1947.

Prelims focus

  • March 1946: Cabinet Mission arrived in India.
  • 16 May 1946: Cabinet Mission issued its constitutional statement.
  • 3 central subjects: Foreign affairs, defence and communications.
  • 3 provincial sections: A, B and C.
  • Residuary powers: Proposed to remain with the provinces.
  • Trap: The Cabinet Mission Plan proposed a united constitutional arrangement, not the Partition settlement of 1947.

[UK Parliament, Hansard, India: Statement by the Cabinet Mission, 16 May 1946, especially paragraphs 15–20; UK Parliament, Hansard, Indian Constitution (Conversations), 11 December 1946; NCERT, Our Pasts III, Class 8, Chapter 9, printed pp. 125–126; Government of India, Publications Division, Towards Independence, section on the Cabinet Mission, online sources consulted 22 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: The Cabinet Mission proposed a limited Union, provincial groups and autonomous provinces.

title: The 1945–46 Elections and the Cabinet Mission Plan
